Chapter 11: Returning to the Source—The Practice of Remembering.
You know, life really does have a way of pulling us in every direction. There’s work, family, and all those little distractions that can easily crowd out what matters most.
That’s why this idea of remembering—returning, again and again, to the source of our strength and peace—is so powerful.
Let me tell you a story. There was a teacher who felt overwhelmed by her job. The passion she used to feel just... faded away, replaced by a sense of dread each morning and exhaustion from endless tasks.
One weekend, she decided to take a walk in the woods—no phone, no distractions. Just her and the trees. And as she walked, something shifted. She remembered why she’d chosen this path in the first place—wanting to make a difference, nurture growth, and share hope. Sure, it was a bittersweet memory, but it rekindled that sense of calling she thought she’d lost.
Isn’t it true? Most of us forget, now and then, what really grounds us. The pressures of daily life can blur the deeper truths that give us meaning and direction. But when we practice remembering—whether it’s through quiet reflection, prayer, or just pausing to notice what’s around us—we find our way back to ourselves, and to the presence that sustains us.
There’s another story—a young couple, busy raising kids and building their careers, suddenly realized they’d drifted apart. So, they made a simple change: one evening a week, just for them. They’d share a meal, talk about their dreams, and remember the love that first brought them together. It wasn’t some grand gesture, but it transformed their relationship.
Here’s something important to remember: this isn’t about living in the past. It’s about returning to the source—the values, the relationships, and that sense of presence that gives life real depth.
After her walk, the teacher approached each day with new energy. The couple, thanks to their weekly ritual, rediscovered the joy in each other’s company.
So, in a world that’s always demanding our attention, the practice of remembering can help us stay rooted. It invites us to live with intention and keep drawing strength from that well inside us—a well that never runs dry.
